missing_spec_content.spec_text: The main energy resources available for use on Earth include: fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas), nuclear fuel, bio-fuel, wind, hydro- electricity, geothermal, the tides, the Sun and water waves.
missing_spec_content.why: Geothermal and water waves are never mentioned. Oil is only named in a list and gets no description, advantages or disadvantages. Bio-fuel is replaced by 'biomass'.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: compare ways that different energy resources are used, the uses to include transport, electricity generation and heating
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson only covers electricity generation. It does not mention using energy resources for transport (for example petrol, diesel or bio-fuels) or for heating (for example gas boilers or solar water heating).

missing_spec_content.spec_text: explain patterns and trends in the use of energy resources.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson gives one snapshot ('UK energy mix (approximate 2023)') and says coal is 'being phased out'. It does not teach the student to explain trends over time, such as the fall in coal, the rise in renewables or changing demand.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: show that science has the ability to identify environmental issues arising from the use of energy resources but not always the power to deal with the issues because of political, social, ethical or economic considerations.
missing_spec_content.why: This is not taught anywhere in the lesson.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: describe the environmental impact arising from the use of different energy resources
missing_spec_content.why: This is only partly covered. The impacts given are mostly CO₂, radioactive waste, visual impact and dam ecosystems. Other impacts are missing, such as sulfur dioxide and acid rain from coal and oil, oil spills, and habitat effects of tidal barrages. Wave and geothermal impacts are absent because those resources are absent.

above_gcse.text: Most traditional power stations work in a chain: - burn fuel (coal, gas, oil), or use nuclear fission (uranium), to release heat - the heat boils water to make steam - the steam drives a turbine - the turbine drives a generator
above_gcse.why: Spec 4.1.3 says 'Descriptions of how energy resources are used to generate electricity are not required.' This whole key point, its writeBullets, keyTerms and checkpoint 3 teach content the specification excludes.

above_gcse.text: The transformer equation: V₁/V₂ = n₁/n₂. That is, primary voltage ÷ secondary voltage = primary turns ÷ secondary turns.
above_gcse.why: Spec 4.2.4.3 says 'The construction and operation of transformers is covered Transformers (HT only)'. The turns-ratio equation is Higher Tier only and is not part of the National Grid section. It could confuse Foundation students. The same applies to checkpoint 1 and examTips[1].

above_gcse.text: For an ideal (100% efficient) transformer: V₁I₁ = V₂I₂ (power in = power out).
above_gcse.why: This is Higher Tier transformer content from a different spec section. It is not required by 4.2.4.3.

above_gcse.text: An AC current in the primary coil makes a changing magnetic field. That changing field induces a voltage in the secondary coil.
above_gcse.why: The spec defers how transformers operate to the separate Higher Tier section. Section 4.2.4.3 only requires knowing that step-up and step-down transformers change the potential difference.

above_gcse.text: The grid needs baseload power (constant and reliable, like nuclear). It needs a peak load response (flexible, like gas).
above_gcse.why: Baseload and peak load are not spec terms. The spec only asks students to 'understand why some energy resources are more reliable than others'.
Solar cell efficiency figures are not required by the specification.

above_gcse.text: Can store energy (pumped hydro); no fuel
above_gcse.why: Pumped storage is not in the specification sections.

above_gcse.text:
400 kV down to 33 kV for heavy industry
- 11 kV for lighter industry
above_gcse.why: The intermediate distribution voltages go beyond the spec. The spec only requires that step-down transformers decrease the potential difference 'to a much lower value' for domestic use.

factual_errors.text: But it is intermittent, and only works when it is sunny.
factual_errors.correction: Solar PV works in any daylight, including cloudy conditions, though output is lower. It produces nothing at night. The lesson's own table correctly says 'Only works in daylight'.

factual_errors.text: UK energy mix (approximate 2023): ~40% renewables (mainly offshore wind), ~40% gas, ~15% nuclear, and the rest other.
factual_errors.correction: UK government (DESNZ) figures for 2023 electricity generation are about 46–47% renewables, about 34–35% gas and about 14% nuclear. Wind as a whole, onshore and offshore together, was the largest renewable share. Calling renewables 'mainly offshore wind' overstates offshore wind's share.
This repeats the inaccurate figures. The 2023 figures are about 47% renewables, about 35% gas and about 14% nuclear.

wrong_terms.text: A step-up transformer then raises this to up to 400,000 V (400 kV). This is for sending it a long way through high-voltage overhead cables. At the other end, a series of step-down transformers lower the voltage in stages
wrong_terms.spec_term: potential difference ("Step-up transformers are used to increase the potential difference")

wrong_terms.text: It increases voltage and decreases current.
Energy sources — comparison for the national grid
Energy source that is naturally replenished and will not run out
wrong_terms.spec_term: energy resource that is being (or can be) replenished as it is used

checkpoint_mismatch.checkpoint: 3: Which energy source can generate electricity without using a turbine?
checkpoint_mismatch.why: Checkpoint 3 sits with keyPoints[3], which covers renewability, reliability and environmental impact. Its answer rests on keyPoints[2] ('Solar PV is the odd one out'), which keyPoints[3] does not mention. No checkpoint tests keyPoints[3]'s own content, and keyPoints[2] has no checkpoint of its own. The question also tests content the spec excludes ('Descriptions of how energy resources are used to generate electricity are not required').

not_checked: All 'diagram' fields are null, so there were no diagrams to check.

examTips[0] claims 'Give both equations for full marks'. I could not check this against mark schemes from the specification text provided. In my understanding, AQA mark schemes credit the explanation (higher p.d., lower current, less heating in cables) without requiring equations.

Cost claims such as 'the cheapest new electricity source in the UK by the 2020s' and 'Coal: ... the cheapest to burn' depend on the date and the source used. They could not be checked against the specification.
